name: Kung (Zu|’Hõasi)
confidence_why: The initial-stress coding rests only on the StressTyp2 and Gordon 2002 survey entries, which take it second-hand from Snyman 1970 (not read), while Downing 2004 reports that Ju|'hoan and the other Khoisan languages are described as tone languages with no discussion of stress in the literature, so the record is a guess until a first-hand description is read.

audit.recode_to: Pending Snyman 1970 / Miller-Ockhuizen 2003: likely 'tone language, no described word stress (root-initial positional prominence only)' rather than fixed-strict initial; at minimum downgrade strength of the evidence and mark domain=root.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the record carries no quotation; the deciding material is StressTyp2 boilerplate for the StressTyp2 entry for this language (source = Snyman 1970, no page, no passage text in the held StressTyp2 SQL dump) plus Gordon 2002's appendix row 'Initial (root) Kung (Zu|'Häası̃) Khoisan', which I confirmed at p.542 of the PDF we hold. We hold no copy of Snyman 1970 or any other primary phonology of Ju|'hoan; the juho1239 files we hold are morphosyntax papers. (2) Deciding source is therefore a database/survey chain resting second-hand on a 1970 introductory grammar. Better descriptions exist and are unheld: Snyman 1975 phonology, Dickens 2005 grammar, Miller-Ockhuizen 2001/2003 instrumental monograph, Pratchett 2017 dissertation. WALS's own prosody chapters (same compilers as StressTyp2) do not code Ju|'hoan for stress at all, only tone. (3) Open copies downloaded now (A. Miller's OSU homepage; ZASPiL): Downing 2004:111-112 explici

sources.note: Treats Ju (incl. Juǀ'hoan) as lexically tonal with tone marked on every cited form; states that Proto-Ju tonology is still poorly understood (p.23), notes Juǀ'hoan's 'rare extra high tone' on !ű 'bone' (p.28), that 'tonal alternations actually exist in Ju' (p.39, on Doke's purely tonal ȕːm 'mountain' vs ūːm 'stone'), and reconstructs ultra-low tone plus breathiness for some roots (pp. 49, 55). No tone inventory or tonal analysis is given.

sources.note: One-paragraph acoustics abstract on consonant-induced F0 lowering after guttural clicks (instrumental, ESPS epochs); says nothing about the lexical tone inventory, TBU or stress.

tone.quote: This study presents the results of an investigation of the fundamental frequency of vowels following guttural clicks in Ju/hoansi. ... The results here show that voicing only lowers fundamental frequency when the release phase of a consonant is voiced as is the case for the voiced aspirated clicks, and not when there is only closure voicing, as is found in the case of the voiced epiglottalized clicks.
